chief_complaint: left upper quadrant pain and low BP after car crash
hpi_details: A 53-year-old male presents to the emergency department with left upper quadrant pain and low blood pressure following a car crash earlier today. He reports the pain began at the time of the crash and has persisted since.
ideas: He thinks the steering wheel or seatbelt just bruised his ribs or cracked a bone on his left side.
concerns: He is worried that he is bleeding out internally from the impact and will not survive emergency surgery.
expectations: He hopes to get a CT scan and intravenous fluids to stabilize his blood pressure and avoid being rushed into surgery.

investigation_events.title: Trauma FAST examination
investigation_events.availability_message: The bedside FAST result is now available; damage-control resuscitation and immediate trauma-surgery involvement should not be delayed for CT in this unstable patient.

results.value: Large volume of free intraperitoneal fluid in the left upper quadrant and pelvis, consistent with hemoperitoneum

clinical_knowledge.topic: Traumatic Splenic Rupture evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Traumatic Splenic Rupture is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management for Traumatic Splenic Rupture emphasizes aggressive fluid/blood resuscitation with laparotomy or embolization as indicated, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: left upper quadrant pain and low BP after car crash

Key HPI features: A 53-year-old male presents with left upper quadrant pain and low blood pressure following a car crash earlier today; the pain began at the time of the crash and has persisted since.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Traumatic Splenic Rupture.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Traumatic Splenic Rupture.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Rib fracture with pulmonary contusion without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Hypotension after trauma — assume ongoing hemorrhage until proven otherwise.
management_principles: Plan for Traumatic Splenic Rupture: Aggressive fluid/blood resuscitation, laparotomy or embolization
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: A 53-year-old male presents with left upper quadrant pain and low blood pressure following a car crash earlier today. He reports the pain began at the time of the crash and has persisted since.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Traumatic Splenic Rupture.
reference_soap.assessment: Assessment consistent with Traumatic Splenic Rupture.
reference_soap.plan: Initiate damage-control resuscitation and obtain immediate trauma-surgery involvement. Hemodynamically unstable patients with suspected splenic hemorrhage need operative control; stable patients may undergo CT-based grading and nonoperative management with angioembolization when indicated.

teaching.one_liner: Blunt abdominal trauma tears the spleen, causing left upper quadrant pain, referred left shoulder pain (Kehr's sign), and hemorrhagic shock.
red_flags: Hypotension after trauma — assume ongoing hemorrhage until proven otherwise

must_ask.say: Can you tell me exactly what happened in the crash?
Where is the pain — is it on your left side, under your ribs?
Does the pain spread to your left shoulder?
Do you feel dizzy or like you might faint?
Did you lose consciousness at any point?

Yes, I feel an ache radiating up into the tip of my left shoulder, especially when I lie back flat.

It was about a 6 out of 10 right after the impact, but now it is an 8 or 9 out of 10.
Any movement, taking a deep breath, or pressing on my left side makes it worse; lying perfectly still with my knees up helps a tiny bit.
No, I have never had any severe abdominal pain or injuries like this before.

No, I have not noticed yellowing of my eyes or skin, and my stool and urine look normal.

I don't have chest pressure or heart pain, but taking a deep breath catches under my left ribs.

exam.finding: Pale, diaphoretic male lying supine in obvious moderate-to-severe distress from abdominal discomfort.
Blood pressure 88/56 mmHg, heart rate 116 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6 C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Marked conjunctival pallor bilaterally; sclerae are non-icteric.
Contusion and focal tenderness over the left lower ribs 9 through 11 without crepitus or bony step-off.
Normal vesicular breath sounds bilaterally without rales, rhonchi, or diminished breath sounds.
Tachycardic rate with regular rhythm; normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Mild fullness and seatbelt contusion across the left upper quadrant without surgical scars or distension.
Hypoactive bowel sounds across all four abdominal quadrants.
Exquisite tenderness and voluntary guarding localized to the left upper quadrant; the remaining quadrants are soft.
Definite rebound tenderness elicited in the left upper quadrant.
Palpation under the left costal margin causes sharp tenderness and reveals fullness; the liver edge is smooth and non-tender.
Normal sphincter tone, no tenderness or palpable mass, and no gross blood on the examining finger.
